section: Present distribution cannot be accounted for by differences in physical conditions
label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
claim: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.
quote: the first great fact which strikes us is, that neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of various regions can be accounted for by their climatal and other physical conditions.
scope: terrestrial and marine faunas and floras of the world's major regions
measurable_quantities: compositional (taxonomic or phylogenetic) similarity between regions
climatic/environmental similarity between regions
candidate_data: Species occurrence data from GBIF and OBIS combined with WorldClim climate layers, and phylogenies from Open Tree of Life, allow partitioning biotic similarity into climatic and geographic/historical components.

section: Importance of barriers
label: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas
claim: Barriers of any kind that obstruct free migration (oceans, isthmuses, mountain ranges, deserts, large rivers) are closely related to the differences between the inhabitants of different regions, and the more impassable and long-standing the barrier, the greater the difference.
quote: A second great fact which strikes us in our general review is, that barriers of any kind, or obstacles to free migration, are related in a close and important manner to the differences between the productions of various regions.
scope: terrestrial and marine organisms across continents, oceans and within continents
measurable_quantities: species turnover (beta diversity) across barriers versus across equal distances without barriers
barrier type and estimated age
candidate_data: GBIF and OBIS occurrence records with biogeographic regionalisations (e.g. Holt et al. 2013 zoogeographic regions) and phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree, including the well-studied trans-Isthmian marine species pairs.

section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
label: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations
claim: The inhabitants of the same continent or sea show a pervasive affinity to one another, so that distinct but related species replace one another from place to place and across different habitats, rather than being replaced by forms from other continents living under similar conditions.
quote: A third great fact, partly included in the foregoing statements, is the affinity of the productions of the same continent or sea, though the species themselves are distinct at different points and stations.
scope: species assemblages within continents and seas
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of co-continental species versus species from other continents in similar habitats
candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree combined with GBIF distributions allow testing whether species are phylogenetically clustered by continent more than by habitat or climate.

section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
label: The bond linking inhabitants of the same area through space and time is inheritance
claim: The deep affinity uniting the living and extinct inhabitants of the same area, independent of physical conditions, is due to inheritance from common ancestors, while the differences among regions arise mainly from modification through natural selection and only subordinately from the direct influence of physical conditions.
quote: This bond, on my theory, is simply inheritance, that cause which alone, as far as we positively know, produces organisms quite like, or, as we see in the case of varieties nearly like each other.
scope: all organisms within a geographic area, living and fossil
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic clustering of species by region
relatedness of fossil and living species from the same region
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database can test whether regional biotas form clades and whether fossil forms of a region are related to its living forms.

section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
label: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification
claim: Migration and isolation do not by themselves cause modification; a group of competing species that migrates together into a new, isolated country will be little modified, because modification is driven by organisms being brought into new relations with one another.
quote: If, for instance, a number of species, which stand in direct competition with each other, migrate in a body into a new and afterwards isolated country, they will be little liable to modification; for neither migration nor isolation in themselves can do anything.
scope: species colonising new isolated areas
measurable_quantities: degree of phenotypic or taxonomic divergence after colonisation
change in the community of competitors experienced by colonists
candidate_data: Comparative studies of island and introduced populations, and experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. on Dryad) that manipulate community composition, could bear on it.

section: Centres of creation
label: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there
claim: Each species was first produced in one area only and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence allowed under past and present conditions, rather than arising independently at several points.
quote: Hence it seems to me, as it has to many other naturalists, that the view of each species having been produced in one area alone, and having subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence under past and present conditions permitted, is the most probable.
scope: all species
measurable_quantities: monophyly of conspecific populations across disjunct ranges
geographic origin inferred from phylogeographic structure
candidate_data: Phylogeographic sequence data in GenBank and population-genetic datasets on Dryad allow testing whether disjunct populations of a species share a single geographic origin.

section: Centres of creation
label: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local
claim: Some families, many sub-families, very many genera and still more sections of genera are confined to a single region, and the most natural genera (those whose species are most closely related) are generally confined to one area.
quote: Some few families, many sub-families, very many genera, and a still greater number of sections of genera are confined to a single region; and it has been observed by several naturalists, that the most natural genera, or those genera in which the species are most closely related to each other, are generally local, or confined to one area.
scope: higher taxa (families, genera, sections) of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: proportion of taxa endemic to one region at each taxonomic rank
geographic range size of a genus versus the phylogenetic age or tightness of its species
candidate_data: GBIF distributions linked to taxonomic backbones and dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) allow measuring regional endemism by rank and its relation to clade age.

section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
label: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period
claim: Although continents have undergone great oscillations of level, separate continents have not been continuously joined to each other and to the existing oceanic islands within the period of existing species, contrary to the land-bridge hypotheses of Forbes and others.
quote: But I do not believe that it will ever be proved that within the recent period continents which are now quite separate, have been continuously, or almost continuously, united with each other, and with the many existing oceanic islands.
scope: continents and oceanic islands during the period of existing species
measurable_quantities: bathymetric depth between islands and continents
geological age and origin (volcanic versus continental) of oceanic islands
past land connections reconstructed from sea-level history
candidate_data: GEBCO bathymetry, radiometric ages of oceanic islands from the geological literature, and plate-reconstruction and sea-level records bear directly on it.

section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
label: About a tenth of a flora's seeds could survive sea-drift across 900 miles
claim: Based on flotation and germination experiments, the seeds of roughly 10 per cent of the plants of a flora, after drying, could be floated by sea currents across about 900 miles of sea and still germinate.
quote: Therefore it would perhaps be safer to assume that the seeds of about 10/100 plants of a flora, after having been dried, could be floated across a space of sea 900 miles in width, and would then germinate.
scope: seeds and fruits of flowering plants exposed to sea-water
measurable_quantities: proportion of species whose diaspores float for a given duration
germination after sea-water immersion
ocean current speeds
candidate_data: Seed-buoyancy trait records (e.g. in the LEDA Traitbase) and published sea-water immersion experiments, combined with ocean-current data, could test the estimate.

section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
label: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents
claim: Occasional means of transport (sea currents, birds, drift timber, icebergs) suffice to carry organisms across a few hundred miles of sea, between islands or from a continent to a nearby island, but not between distant continents, so the floras of distant continents remain distinct.
quote: These means, however, would suffice for occasional transport across tracts of sea some hundred miles in breadth, or from island to island, or from a continent to a neighbouring island, but not from one distant continent to another.
scope: plants (and by extension other organisms) dispersing across seas
measurable_quantities: frequency of long-distance dispersal events by distance
shared species between land masses as a function of separation distance
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree) used to infer oceanic dispersal events, and island floras in GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) against distance to source, could test it.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period
claim: The same arctic and alpine species on widely separated mountain summits and in arctic regions are relicts of populations that spread across the intervening lowlands during the Glacial period and were stranded on mountains and in the far north as the climate warmed.
quote: Hence, when the warmth had fully returned, the same arctic species, which had lately lived in a body together on the lowlands of the Old and New Worlds, would be left isolated on distant mountain-summits (having been exterminated on all lesser heights) and in the arctic regions of both hemispheres.
scope: arctic-alpine plants and animals of Europe and North America
measurable_quantities: phylogeographic divergence times among mountain populations
fossil and pollen records of arctic species in now-temperate lowlands during glacials
candidate_data: Neotoma Paleoecology Database pollen and macrofossil records together with phylogeographic sequence data in GenBank for arctic-alpine species.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land
claim: The relationship, with very little identity, between the temperate inhabitants of North America and Europe arises because a common biota inhabited the nearly continuous circumpolar land in warmer Pliocene times and then migrated southward, becoming separated and modified on each continent.
quote: On this view we can understand the relationship, with very little identity, between the productions of North America and Europe,—a relationship which is most remarkable, considering the distance of the two areas, and their separation by the Atlantic Ocean.
scope: temperate plants and animals of North America and Europe
measurable_quantities: divergence times of intercontinental sister taxa
fossil occurrences of shared taxa at high northern latitudes in the Pliocene and earlier Tertiary
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies from TimeTree and fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database can test the timing and high-latitude route of North American–European disjunctions.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
claim: The Glacial period, which lasted a very long time at each place, was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, or at least along broad longitudinal belts from pole to pole, so that global temperature was lower at the same time.
quote: If this be admitted, it is difficult to avoid believing that the temperature of the whole world was at this period simultaneously cooler.
scope: global climate during the most recent glacial period
measurable_quantities: timing of glacial maxima in both hemispheres
paleotemperature records from tropical and polar regions
candidate_data: Ice-core records (e.g. EPICA Dome C), the LR04 benthic oxygen-isotope stack, and NOAA paleoclimate archives document the timing of glacial cooling worldwide.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related
claim: Throughout the world, plants growing on high mountains (including tropical ones) and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres are sometimes identical species but much more often distinct yet closely related species.
quote: Hence we see that throughout the world, the plants growing on the more lofty mountains, and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres, are sometimes identically the same; but they are much oftener specifically distinct, though related to each other in a most remarkable manner.
scope: flowering plants of temperate lowlands and tropical and temperate mountains
measurable_quantities: number of species and genera shared between northern temperate, tropical montane and southern temperate floras
phylogenetic relatedness of these floras
candidate_data: Plant occurrence and floristic data from GBIF, BIEN and GIFT combined with plant phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Glacial interchange ran mainly north to south because northern forms were more dominant
claim: Many more identical and allied plant forms migrated from north to south during the Glacial period than in the reverse direction, because the greater land area of the north and the larger populations there had made northern forms more advanced and dominant through natural selection and competition.
quote: I suspect that this preponderant migration from north to south is due to the greater extent of land in the north, and to the northern forms having existed in their own homes in greater numbers, and having consequently been advanced through natural selection and competition to a higher stage of perfection or dominating power, than the southern forms.
scope: plants migrating between hemispheres during the Glacial period
measurable_quantities: number of north-to-south versus south-to-north dispersal events inferred from phylogenies
land area and population size of source regions
candidate_data: Biogeographic reconstructions on dated plant phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with GBIF distributions can count the direction of inter-hemispheric dispersal events.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
claim: At the present day many European species have become naturalised and partly displaced the natives in La Plata and to a lesser degree in Australia, whereas extremely few southern-hemisphere species have become naturalised anywhere in Europe.
quote: Just in the same manner as we see at the present day, that very many European productions cover the ground in La Plata, and in a lesser degree in Australia, and have to a certain extent beaten the natives; whereas extremely few southern forms have become naturalised in any part of Europe,
scope: naturalised plants and animals exchanged between Europe and southern-hemisphere regions
measurable_quantities: number of species naturalised from Europe in South America and Australia
number of species naturalised from southern regions in Europe
candidate_data: The Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF) database and DAISIE European alien-species inventories record donor and recipient regions of naturalised species.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period
claim: Distinct species of genera confined to the southern hemisphere spread in radiating lines from the antarctic lands, which supported a peculiar flora during a warmer period before the Glacial period, reaching southern America, Australia and New Zealand by occasional transport and former islands.
quote: I am inclined to look in the southern, as in the northern hemisphere, to a former and warmer period, before the commencement of the Glacial period, when the antarctic lands, now covered with ice, supported a highly peculiar and isolated flora.
scope: southern-hemisphere plant genera with disjunct distributions
measurable_quantities: fossil plant occurrences in Antarctica
divergence times and inferred ancestral areas of southern disjunct clades
candidate_data: Antarctic fossil plant occurrences in the Paleobiology Database and dated phylogenies of southern clades (e.g. via TimeTree) bear on it.

section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
label: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide
claim: Despite being separated by land and sea barriers, many fresh-water species of quite different classes have enormous ranges, and allied fresh-water species prevail throughout the world.
quote: Not only have many fresh-water species, belonging to quite different classes, an enormous range, but allied species prevail in a remarkable manner throughout the world.
scope: fresh-water plants and animals (insects, molluscs, plants, etc.)
measurable_quantities: geographic range size of fresh-water versus terrestrial species in the same groups
number of continents occupied by fresh-water genera
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence records and freshwater-specific compilations (e.g. Freshwater Ecoregions of the World, IUCN Red List freshwater assessments) can compare range sizes of aquatic and terrestrial taxa.

section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
claim: The same species of fresh-water fish never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents, although within a continent fish species often range widely and irregularly, different river systems sharing some species but not others.
quote: In regard to fish, I believe that the same species never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents. But on the same continent the species often range widely and almost capriciously; for two river-systems will have some fish in common and some different.
scope: fresh-water fishes
measurable_quantities: number of strictly fresh-water fish species native to more than one continent
species overlap between river basins within a continent
candidate_data: FishBase distribution records and global freshwater fish occurrence-by-drainage-basin compilations, together with GBIF, can test both parts.

section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
label: Water birds disperse seeds and eggs, explaining wide ranges of fresh-water life
claim: The wide distribution of fresh-water plants and lower fresh-water animals depends mainly on the transport of their seeds and eggs by animals, especially wide-flying fresh-water birds that move between often distant bodies of water.
quote: But the wide distribution of fresh-water plants and of the lower animals, whether retaining the same identical form or in some degree modified, I believe mainly depends on the wide dispersal of their seeds and eggs by animals, more especially by fresh-water birds, which have large powers of flight, and naturally travel from one to another and often distant piece of water.
scope: fresh-water plants and small fresh-water invertebrates
measurable_quantities: frequency of viable propagules carried externally or internally by waterbirds
waterbird movement distances
genetic connectivity of aquatic populations along flyways
candidate_data: Waterbird tracking data in Movebank and published waterbird propagule-transport studies, with population-genetic data in GenBank or Dryad for aquatic plants and invertebrates.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas
claim: Oceanic islands are inhabited by far fewer species of all kinds than continental areas of equal size, a difference not explained by physical conditions.
quote: The species of all kinds which inhabit oceanic islands are few in number compared with those on equal continental areas
scope: plants and animals of oceanic islands compared with continental areas
measurable_quantities: native species richness per unit area on oceanic islands versus continental samples of equal area
candidate_data: Island and mainland checklists in GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) and GBIF allow species-area comparisons between oceanic islands and continental regions.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
claim: Although oceanic islands have few species, the proportion of their species that are endemic (found nowhere else) is often extremely large relative to their area, as expected if occasional colonists arriving in a new isolated district are especially liable to modification.
quote: Although in oceanic islands the number of kinds of inhabitants is scanty, the proportion of endemic species (_i.e._ those found nowhere else in the world) is often extremely large.
scope: plants and animals of oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: proportion of endemic species on oceanic islands
endemic species per unit area on islands versus continents
candidate_data: GIFT island floras with endemism status, IUCN Red List and BirdLife range data for vertebrates, and GBIF occurrences.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Island endemism is low in groups that arrive easily and in numbers
claim: Within one island, some groups are almost wholly endemic while others are not, because groups that immigrate readily and in a body (e.g. marine birds, sea-shells, regularly visiting land-birds) keep their mutual relations undisturbed and so are little modified.
quote: But it by no means follows, that, because in an island nearly all the species of one class are peculiar, those of another class, or of another section of the same class, are peculiar; and this difference seems to depend on the species which do not become modified having immigrated with facility and in a body, so that their mutual relations have not been much disturbed.
scope: groups of organisms on oceanic islands differing in dispersal ability
measurable_quantities: proportion of endemic species per taxonomic group on an island
dispersal ability or immigration frequency of each group
candidate_data: Island checklists with endemism status (GIFT, BirdLife, IUCN Red List) combined with dispersal traits (e.g. AVONET hand-wing index for birds) allow testing whether endemism declines with dispersal ability.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees
claim: Because trees rarely reach distant oceanic islands, herbaceous plants that colonise them gain an advantage by growing taller, so natural selection often converts insular herbaceous plants first into bushes and then into trees, explaining why islands have trees in orders that are elsewhere herbaceous.
quote: If so, natural selection would often tend to add to the stature of herbaceous plants when growing on an island, to whatever order they belonged, and thus convert them first into bushes and ultimately into trees.
scope: flowering plants on oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: frequency of derived woodiness in island versus mainland lineages
phylogenetic transitions from herbaceous to woody growth form
candidate_data: Global compilations of derived insular woodiness from the botanical literature, combined with plant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) and growth-form data in the TRY plant trait database.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
claim: Batrachians (frogs, toads and newts) are naturally absent from oceanic islands, not because conditions there are unsuitable (introduced frogs thrive) but because they and their spawn are killed by sea-water and so cannot cross the sea.
quote: Bory St. Vincent long ago remarked that Batrachians (frogs, toads, newts) have never been found on any of the many islands with which the great oceans are studded. I have taken pains to verify this assertion, and I have found it strictly true.
scope: amphibians on oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: presence of native amphibian species on oceanic islands
establishment success of introduced amphibians on oceanic islands
candidate_data: AmphibiaWeb and IUCN Red List amphibian range maps, plus GBIF records and island geological origin, can test native amphibian occurrence on oceanic islands.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent
claim: No native terrestrial mammal inhabits any island more than about 300 miles from a continent or large continental island, even though small mammals thrive when introduced there, because terrestrial mammals cannot cross wide stretches of sea.
quote: as yet I have not found a single instance, free from doubt, of a terrestrial mammal (excluding domesticated animals kept by the natives) inhabiting an island situated above 300 miles from a continent or great continental island;
scope: native non-flying mammals on islands
measurable_quantities: presence of native terrestrial mammals by island isolation distance
establishment of introduced mammals on remote islands
candidate_data: Native mammal ranges from PHYLACINE or IUCN Red List range maps, overlaid with island locations and distance to mainland.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
claim: Although terrestrial mammals are absent from oceanic islands, bats occur on almost every island, and remote islands often have their own endemic bat species, because bats can fly across wide spaces of sea and are then modified in their new homes.
quote: Though terrestrial mammals do not occur on oceanic islands, ærial mammals do occur on almost every island.
scope: bats on oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: presence and number of native bat species on oceanic islands
proportion of island bat species that are endemic
candidate_data: IUCN Red List and PHYLACINE bat range data combined with island geography, and GBIF occurrence records.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity
claim: Somewhat independently of distance, the depth of sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland is related to whether they share the same or allied mammal species: islands separated by shallow channels have the same or very similar mammals, those across deep water have distinct species and genera.
quote: there is also a relation, to a certain extent independent of distance, between the depth of the sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland, and the presence in both of the same mammiferous species or of allied species in a more or less modified condition.
scope: terrestrial mammals of continental and near-continental islands
measurable_quantities: depth of the channel between island and mainland
proportion of island mammal species shared with or congeneric with the mainland
island–mainland distance
candidate_data: GEBCO bathymetry combined with mammal ranges from PHYLACINE or IUCN Red List and a mammal phylogeny (e.g. via Open Tree of Life).

section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
label: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent
claim: It is an almost universal rule that the endemic species of islands are related to those of the nearest continent or other nearby islands, even when the islands' physical conditions resemble those of a different, more distant region (e.g. Galapagos to America, Cape Verde to Africa).
quote: indeed it is an almost universal rule that the endemic productions of islands are related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands.
scope: endemic plants and animals of oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: geographic location of the closest relatives (sister lineages) of island endemics
distance from island to the source region versus to the nearest continent
candidate_data: Phylogenies in Open Tree of Life and sequence data in GenBank, combined with GBIF distributions, allow identifying the source region of island endemic lineages.

section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
label: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other
claim: The distinct species inhabiting the separate islands of an archipelago are far more closely related to one another than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world, because the islands received immigrants from the same source or from each other.
quote: so that the inhabitants of each separate island, though mostly distinct, are related in an incomparably closer degree to each other than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world.
scope: endemic species of oceanic archipelagos
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness among species on different islands of an archipelago versus to mainland species
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of archipelago radiations from GenBank and Open Tree of Life (e.g. Galapagos finches and mockingbirds).

section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
label: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join
claim: Species that become naturalised in new countries are generally not closely allied to the native inhabitants but are very distinct, often belonging to genera absent from the region, whereas closely allied species equally well fitted to their places tend to keep separate.
quote: the forms which become naturalised in new countries are not generally closely allied to the aboriginal inhabitants, but are very distinct species, belonging in a large proportion of cases, as shown by Alph. de Candolle, to distinct genera.
scope: naturalised (introduced) plants and animals
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between naturalised species and the native flora or fauna
proportion of naturalised species belonging to genera not native to the region
candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-plant records combined with regional native floras (GIFT) and plant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) allow direct tests.

section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
label: Inhabitants of any area are modified colonists from the most accessible source
claim: The inhabitants of any area (oceanic islands, mountains, lakes, marshes, caves), where not identical, are plainly related to those of the region from which colonists could most readily have come, the colonists having since been modified and better fitted to their new homes.
quote: The principle which determines the general character of the fauna and flora of oceanic islands, namely, that the inhabitants, when not identically the same, yet are plainly related to the inhabitants of that region whence colonists could most readily have been derived,—the colonists having been subsequently modified and better fitted to their new homes,—is of the widest application throughout nature.
scope: biotas of islands, mountains, lakes, marshes and caves
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of alpine, cave or lake species to species of surrounding lowlands versus distant similar habitats
candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life and GenBank sequences for alpine, cave and lake lineages, combined with GBIF distributions of their relatives.

section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
label: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species
claim: Wherever two regions, however distant, contain many closely allied or representative species, they will also contain some identical species and many doubtful forms ranked variously as species or varieties, showing past migration between them.
quote: And it will, I believe, be universally found to be true, that wherever in two regions, let them be ever so distant, many closely allied or representative species occur, there will likewise be found some identical species
scope: pairs of geographic regions with related biotas
measurable_quantities: number of allied (congeneric) species shared between two regions
number of identical species shared between the same regions
candidate_data: GBIF occurrences or regional checklists (e.g. GIFT for plants) can measure the correlation between shared congeners and shared species across region pairs.

section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
label: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range
claim: Organisms lower in the scale of nature tend to range more widely than higher ones, because they change more slowly and their seeds and eggs are minute and suited to distant transport.
quote: namely, that the lower any group of organisms is, the more widely it is apt to range.
scope: plants and animals across taxonomic groups considered 'lower' and 'higher'
measurable_quantities: geographic range size of species or genera by group
rate of morphological change by group
propagule size
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence-derived range sizes across major groups, with Paleobiology Database species durations as a proxy for rate of change.

section: Summary
label: Closer relatives tend to be closer together in time and space
claim: Because forms within each class are connected by ordinary generation, the more closely two forms are related by descent, the nearer they will generally be to each other in time and in geographic space.
quote: and the more nearly any two forms are related in blood, the nearer they will generally stand to each other in time and space;
scope: all organisms, living and fossil
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between species pairs
geographic distance between their ranges
stratigraphic separation between fossil taxa
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with GBIF range data and Paleobiology Database occurrences allow testing the correlation of phylogenetic with geographic and temporal distance.
